title: Able or label?
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien argues against flagging students as tier 2 or tier 3 learners to staff, on the ground that labels lower expectations and misdescribe how support needs actually work. He explains that tier 2 membership is not stable, since any student can need extra scaffolding on a given day, so a fixed list lets learning fall through the cracks. He says labels risk an unconscious ceiling on expectations and criticizes ability-grouped task streaming as a mutation of Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. For tier 3 needs he allows that specialist information is useful but insists expectations stay the same, and he notes that most specialist recommendations are already features of explicit instruction. He concludes teachers should drop the labels and assume every student can meet high expectations. His stance is a firm, explicit-instruction position, argued from experience rather than cited studies.
points: Tier 2 status is a daily condition rather than a fixed trait, so flagging a list of students means a usually reliable student having a bad day gets no support.
Labels create unconscious bias and quietly cap expectations, which widens the achievement gap the label was meant to close.
Streaming tasks into high, medium and low groups often leaves low-group students checked off on easy questions while the goalposts never move.

Many specialist recommendations for tier 3 needs, such as chunking, worked examples and checks for understanding, are already core explicit instruction, so well-planned lessons reduce the need for labels.
Brien keeps knowing a functional need (for example a visual impairment) for planning but holds that it must not change the expectations for the student.
quotes: When we label students we are risking putting a ceiling on their potential. This is not done intentionally, however our unconscious biases can then change our treatment of these students and avoid truly challenging and pushing them in their learning.

This is where the problem lies. These students are not the same every single time. On any given day our students come into class with a wide variety of external factors which impact their attention and memory on that day.
The reality however, is that students in the low group complete the low questions, get checked off by the teacher and the goal posts never move. They never improve. Never grow.
However, this label should not change the same high expectations you should have for that student as you would have for any other student.

A further thought on the majority of learning functional needs at a tier 3 level, the large majority of specialist recommendations in managing learning and attention are exactly the core principles of explicit instruction such as chunking information, providing scaffolds, worked examples, checks for understanding, modeling, routines and minimizing transitions. Therefore a well structured and planned explicit lesson removes the need to label these students with additional learning needs at all because their needs are met by great teaching.

All of these labels just place a limit on our students by creating an unconscious bias which means we treat them differently, we do not have the same expectations and therefore do not push them to achieve the same outcomes.

These labels set to separate and alienate these students when we want them to feel like a high quality plain t-shirt. They are reliable, fit right in with the rest of the outfit, sometimes need some additional support (stain removal and ironing) which with that support they will lead to a successful outfit time and time again.
